utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. For Court and counsel, we were up to, by my note, paragraph 54 of the outline.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness J, we had worked our way up into essentially a chronological point of the story, to January of 1993, and I would like to spend a few minutes on that, please. Would it be your testimony today, sir, that in January 1993, the Muslims in Busovaca could not move around but the only people or forces which essentially had freedom of movement was the HVO police and soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, correct. Though some of us could move a little, we sought not to be seen by them. But as soon as there was one, two, or three men together, it was impossible. It was prohibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the night of the 21st of January, 1993. Is it correct that Mirsad Delija was killed when HVO soldiers knocked on his door, and when Delija went out on the balcony to see who was knocking, he was shot and killed or perhaps subsequently died from those wounds?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is right. He was killed immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, on that same evening, is it correct that you were home with your family in your house in Busovaca watching television around 10.15, you heard footsteps outside your home, and then there was a strong explosion that shattered a large window in your living room, and about the time that you and your family were trying to escape from the house, the front door was broken in by people who identified themselves as HVO police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that was exactly how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did these HVO police officers fire shots into your house? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it also correct, Witness J, that in the process of leaving the house, you were able to fire some shots from a weapon back, and that you and your family were able to escape and spent the night in some surrounding woods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Exactly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, later on during that same evening, is it correct, Witness J, that while you could not identify the particular individuals doing the looting and you could not see the patches or insignia, you did see that they were wearing camouflage uniforms, and by their statements among themselves, identified themselves as HVO military police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it is true that I couldn't see, but I was able to gather that from their cries and shouts, "This is the HVO police. Open up." And then they started shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During that same time, is it correct that they stole a number of items from your house, including your Volkswagen Golf car and various household appliances?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. They, in fact, took everything. They moved me out. There was nothing left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, later that same night, at about 3.00 in the morning on what actually would have been then the 22nd of January, 1993, is it correct that you saw three men in uniform again come to your house in what you believe was probably a black Mercedes and also entered the house and, to your observation, took items from the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, about 3.00. That is what they did. They probably picked up what little was left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then later on the morning of the 22nd of January, you were able to return to your house and then see firsthand that essentially all of your property had been stolen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On the 23rd of January, was this same house of yours riddled with gunfire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was. It was riddled with bullets from a distance of about 20 or 30 metres from the road. It was clearly visible where the shots were coming from because there were casings on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Later during the night of the 22nd or 23rd of January, were you able to see other HVO looting going on in the town of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On the same night -- excuse me, I'm sorry -- did the HVO blow up two coffee shops in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: They did. They blew up two coffee shops, and the next night, there were more and more planted mines, so that the nights were very difficult to live through. The days were, after all, a little easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I direct your attention to the night of the 23rd and 24th of January, 1993. Did something happen to your house on that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. It was set on fire. Explosives were placed, there was a strong explosion, and it burned down very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that this was the first Muslim house destroyed in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: The first Muslim house in the town of Busovaca, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is the same house which you testified on Thursday was approximately 150 metres from Dario Kordic's house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Roughly so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you have any information, sir, as to who participated in blowing up and/or burning down your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: A white car was seen at Dario's brother's place, and with him was Aleksandar Ruzic, known as Aco, and some other, to me, unknown people, but these two I knew, and they set fire to the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You said that a white car was seen. What is the significance -- I'm not sure from your answer just now the significance of the white car is clear. Why is that important?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Because, in those days, such a car was driven only by Dario's brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was that car seen at your house at the time it was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it was seen. It was seen by my brother-in-law, my wife's brother, whose house is only 10 metres away from mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Later on that same night, two more Muslim shops in Busovaca were blown up and destroyed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Every night, one or two business premises were blown up. Hand grenades were thrown in, they were looted; everything was taken from them. And this went on until the night of the 25th. This happened every evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Is it fair to say that on the night of the 25th of January, 1993, or it could have been the night between, if you will, the 24th and 25th of January, that most of what were the then remaining Muslim shops in Busovaca were blown up and looted, including your shop?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they were all blown up and looted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall how your shop in particular was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: With a hand grenade. They threw in a bomb. It was an ordinary house whereas the premises that we owned in the centre of town and a relative of mine who had premises right next to mine, his were also destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention then to that following morning, on the 25th of January. Is it correct, sir, that at about 5.30 or 6.00 that morning, a fire siren sounded in Busovaca, and then there was a lot of shooting, and it came to your attention or knowledge at that time and later that morning that there were a number of snipers firing in the town and also there was some artillery shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The siren sounded, and as soon as it stopped, terrible gunfire broke out from all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you able to see from where you were on the morning of the 25th the HVO soldiers attacking Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: It could be seen. It could be seen that there were snipers in the surrounding buildings, and from the surrounding hills, one could also see an anti-aircraft machine gun being brought in a truck behind the old school and the shooting going on from all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you able to identify that morning, or during the day of the 25th of January, various units, military units or formations based upon the insignia or patches that you saw on uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: On that morning, no, but when we had been forced to the square in the centre of Busovaca, then one could see and I could see insignia of the HV army, HVO, HOS, and the Runolist Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you have any information as to where the Runolist Brigade was from? Where were they based?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't know, but they were clearly not from our part of the country because their accent was quite different. From their accent, one could tell that they came from Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you find it to be generally the case, in the instances that you've testified about on Thursday last week and again today, that whenever there was an HVO action, say in Busovaca, that to your knowledge, generally there would be forces and components of HVO forces from outside Busovaca as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct. They all took part, from Vitez, Travnik, Kiseljak, Herzegovina, and I don't know from where else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask the usher, please, to show you Exhibits Z1529 and 2564.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: These have been distributed previously, Your Honour, I believe, in terms of work copies for counsel and the Court.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, let me direct your attention, first of all, to Exhibit 1529. Did you see that patch or insignia on the 25th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you -- I'm sorry. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Can you use the ELMO, please, for the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I didn't look up. I thought it was on. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. So, to go back in terms of what is on the ELMO, Witness J, a moment ago we referred to 1529. That is the patch, as we look at the screen, that is on the right; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On the 25th of January, 1993, did you also see the patch which on the same visual is marked as 2564?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You saw both those patches, in fact, on the 25th of January in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Could we have some more precision from the witness? This badge of the Croatian army and of the HVO, the Bosnian Croat army, if one can call them that, were these badges worn by the same people at the same time, by different people, and what was the proportion, if the witness could tell us? Which was more dominant, those who wore one or the other? So could we have a little more detail, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness J, you've heard Judge Bennouna's questions. When you saw these patches on uniforms, were they -- is it the case that both patches would be on the same uniform, for instance, one on each shoulder, or did you see one patch essentially per uniform or per person, if you will?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Each person had only one badge, either the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, or the HV army. The HVO was the far more numerous. There were far more of those insignia, whereas there were only a few with the insignia of the HV army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as you were in town -- is it true that you were being, essentially, the population -- or much of the Muslim population of Busovaca was being gathered together or collected, if you will, and driven toward the square in the middle of town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: One couldn't really say the majority. At that moment there were some 90 of us gathered in the square, and by then they had covered almost all the other streets and the Mahala. They were already closed or, rather, shut up at Kaonik. So we were among the last, some 90 of us, who were the last who remained, and we were forced to gather in the square.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. When you mention "Mahala," was that a Muslim district, if you will, part of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. The area where we were was inhabited exclusively by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As these events were happening on the 25th of January, is it correct that you saw Muslim women and children leaving their houses about the same time that the HVO soldiers would be seen setting the houses on fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. There was general fear and panic everywhere, so that the entire population moved towards the centre of town, the square, and they were followed by soldiers who were torching houses one after another, so that about 15 houses were burnt on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know whether some Muslim civilians were wounded and some killed on that day, the 25th of January?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. There were many. That is the hardest part. A sniper from the nearby house killed Sedin Merdan. Just a moment, please. Then on that occasion also Irhad Ekmecic was killed. In the streets bodies were seen of Nedzad Navolic, Nihad Merdan, Amir Hodzic. In one house at the other end of town three young men were killed in the same room, Nijaz Neslanovic, the young Hadzibegovic, and a third whose name I cannot recollect. On the bridge, Sunulahpasic, Medju Seliac, and a maths teacher was killed somewhere near the police station. I know that we called him Budo. Then Jahic, a man of 50 to 55 was killed on the road towards Kaonik, somewhere halfway there, near the Vatrostalna factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Can you tell the court, was there any armed resistance to the HVO attack on the 25th of January? Was there any organised defence by the Muslims in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not a single shot was fired. There was no reason for such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness J, were you regarded at that time as a wealthy or prominent member of the Busovaca community?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: One could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And were you, on the 25th of January, acting and existing only in a civilian capacity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. We were all civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would it be your testimony today, sir, that as these events were unfolding, various of the Muslim men, including yourself, were yelling and asking for the HVO to stop their shooting but the soldiers ignored your outcries and continued the shooting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. In spite of all our pleas and cries, they continued shooting until sometime about 3.00 p.m., when there was generalised panic and chaos and when they had forced everyone to the square. Only once we were all there did the shooting stop, and they celebrated this as a victory by hugging and kissing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, please, what happened once the approximately 90 of you were gathered in the square.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: In a couple of minutes a bus appeared, and we were all loaded on to the bus and driven to Kaonik, to the camp there, to a hangar. These were military hangars. When we got there, there was some people there already, so that at one point there were as many as 300 of us in one hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness J, before we get into details of the camp itself, let me ask you a couple more questions. When you were in the square, was there an effort to separate the Muslim men from the women and children who at that time were still a part of that group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. All the men were separated, and the women and children were returned to their homes and we were put on the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In terms of the male Muslims, if you will, who were taken to Kaonik, did that include men as young as 14, 15, and 16 years of age?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were some.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived in the square, can you tell the Court anything you recall about the buses? Did the buses come after you were already in the square, or were the buses -- well, tell the Court what you remember about the buses.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: The bus arrived within a minute or two, which means it must have been parked somewhere there and it was just waiting for us to be rounded up in the centre, in the square, and to be picked up. The bus was driven by Zeljko Vareskovic, known as "Bubreg" or "Kidney."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that Kaonik camp is approximately 5 kilometres from Busovaca and it took you approximately ten minutes to be taken there on the bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Something like that, yes. Five kilometres and about a ten-minute drive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct that the guards at Kaonik camp wore camouflage uniforms with HVO patches and, to your knowledge, were some of the HVO guards from Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. You testified a moment ago that when you arrived there, you were taken -- you and the other prisoners were taken to a hangar. Was this hangar approximately 20 metres wide and 50 to 70 metres long?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you come to know about that time that the commander of the prison camp was a Zlatko Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, we learnt that there because we were lined up facing the wall, one against the other, all pushed up against each other. At one point, we were ordered to turn towards the centre, and a man was standing in the centre who introduced himself and said, "I am Zlatko Aleksovski. I am the commander of the prison. Don't be afraid. You won't be harmed. Not a hair on your head will be harmed."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And this was on the 25th of January; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can just jump ahead in order to put some time boundaries on the next series of events. You were then released from Kaonik on about the 8th of February, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, exactly on February the 8th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, based upon this approximately, let's call it two weeks, two-and-a-half-week period, did you come to know during that time whether Mr. Aleksovski reported or took direction from someone above him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was your understanding about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Aleksovski only executed orders, and on one occasion when we were lined up or, that is to say, when we had returned from digging on one occasion and were lined up in front of the hangar, in front of the prison, we were already down in the cells, in the prison, and when a young man whom we called Pedja came and he asked Aleksovski for 30 prisoners, to give him 30 prisoners to go and do digging, and he gave him a piece of paper, and when Mr. Aleksovski looked at the piece of paper, he told him verbatim that he couldn't get these prisoners because the paper was not signed either by Kordic or by Sliskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness J --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Gudelj told him --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness J, I'm going to stop you there momentarily only for the convenience of the Court and counsel. It is not a problem, but just so that everyone is clear. The witness has jumped ahead to material that is covered starting at paragraph 155. It doesn't really matter when we cover it, but just for the Court's reference, that's where it can be found. All right. Witness J, I apologise. I cut you off. You said that Mr. Aleksovski responded to this HVO officer that the 30 prisoners could not be released unless he had a signed paper by either Mr. Kordic or Mr. Sliskovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What did this officer then reply or say to Mr. Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: His answer was that he wasn't taking away people, he was taking away cattle, and that he didn't have to have anybody's signatures. However, Aleksovski categorically refused to give him the men. Then he left. Some 15 to 20 minutes later, he returned. I did not see that particular paper, but when he handed the paper to Aleksovski, he got his men, which means that it was verified either by Kordic or by Sliskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm going to, with that story in mind, going to go back, and again for the Court and counsel, returning to approximately paragraph 94 or, actually, 95. Is it the case, Witness J, that when you arrived at the prison camp, either at the beginning or throughout your time, to the extent that you still possessed any of these particular items throughout your stay, is it correct that HVO soldiers would take valuables from the Muslim prisoners, such as jewellery, watches, and money?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: They took everything. They took gold and money. And even shoes, if they were good ones; they would take them off too. And fur coats and trousers and anything that was worth anything. They took everything. So that at one point, they had a whole bag full of money.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You testified earlier that by the end of the day on the 25th of January, there were approximately 250 to 300 Muslim men in the hangar at Kaonik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes exactly that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: These prisoners came from such places as Skradno, Loncari, Strane, and Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, from all parts they were brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During this early time -- I'm going to try to skip quickly through the next several paragraphs -- you had very little comforts available to you; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not comforts, it was nothing at all. It was just a concrete floor, and we spent the night on our feet walking about to keep warm because it was the 25th of January, when the nights are very cold in Bosnia, and so we tried to warm up that way and to keep ourselves going, to be alive for the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Even at that early time, is it fair to say that some of the Muslim prisoners were taken out and, when they returned to the larger group, you found that they had been beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That was standard practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me now direct your attention to the following day or days. Either on the 26th or 27th of January, is it correct, sir, that an HVO soldier came into the hangar and read off from a piece of paper a list of 15 names, with your name being approximately the 14th on the list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he read out 15 names. My name was the 14th and my cousin's was the 15th, and we were all taken outside, and when we went out, we saw that they were carrying a rope and started tying us up. We were tied up in the same order in which our names were called out. So that 13 people were tied up. I, as number 14, was not tied up because they didn't have enough rope left, so that I myself and my cousin were not tied, but my brother was tied and other relations, five or six of them, and they were taken off as a human shield, and we were told this straightaway, that we would be going as a human shield because the village of Strane was to be surrounded and was to capitulate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple of details: When you were being tied up, was one of the HVO soldiers the same Zeljko who had driven the bus that you were on to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. It was Zeljko. There was Pusic as well, who was a policeman in the HVO, and there was another person I didn't know but, quite obviously, he was a professional in tying up people because he did it better than the others. And then there were some others standing around, Mirko Cosic, one of them, and, I don't know, some others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In terms of some of the prisoners who were tied up at this time -- I was going to say I would try to read these to save some time, but I'm not sure it would be faster if I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think the names are going to assist us, but the witness's brother was apparently among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He himself was not taken off on this occasion --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I was going to clarify that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- it appears from --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness J, can you clarify for us: You said that you were not tied up because there wasn't enough rope left. Can you clarify whether -- were you, in fact, taken to Strane on this particular occasion or were you left in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I wasn't taken off. I was left in the prison, in the hangar, whereas the 13 of them were taken off.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Those 13 young men were all directly from the town, and they were intentionally, quite obviously, placed on the list and selected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you, but at the time that you said the statement was made, you said there was a clear statement that the intent was to take these men to be used as human shields, that statement was made while you were still in -- excuse me -- while the group was still in camp and you were present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And following the Court's lead, I won't either ask you the name or I won't try to read the individual names, but is it fair to say that all of these were Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Exclusively. Nobody else was held there as prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, there are a couple of other questions I was going to ask you about what happened at Strane, and just so the record is clear, how is it that you have any information about what happened once these prisoners were taken outside the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, after they returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And these are the same men you were in prison with; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: We were all there together in one hangar, and when they returned, they were returned amongst us. We were not in our cells yet. We were all together there in the hangar. We weren't separated at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Did the prisoners, when they returned, tell you that they were used as human shields at the village of Strane where the HVO announced to the Muslims there that if they did not surrender their weapons, these Muslim prisoners would be killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, and according to what my brother said, they were some 15 metres in front of the HVO soldiers facing the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The HVO soldiers being behind them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you for any names or any details of this event, but is it fair to say, do you recall your brother relating to you that one of the HVO soldiers he saw during these events had been the best man at his, your brother's, wedding?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right, and he didn't even look at him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, the following day, were these same men taken and used as human shields again at a location or village called Merdani?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they were. Once again, the same people, the same 13 young men, were taken away once again towards the village of Merdani and, according to what they said, it was ten times worse than the previous day, because they were lined up on the railway bridge and they were threatened that they would be slaughtered if the village of Merdani did not surrender, so that they stayed there the entire day, tied up as a human shield.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, can you tell the Court, about the time that these prisoners were then returned to the camp following this second use as human shields, were you and the others then moved out of the hangar into something that most of us would probably know as a prison cell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, when they returned. And I understood this, and we were all generally happy that they had returned. We were then transferred to the cells below the hangar, which had already been prepared, heaven knows when, and they were intentionally prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did these cells measure approximately three by three metres?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they were three by three, and there were 30 of us, 25, sometimes more in those cells.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you relate to the Court, during this period, once you were put in the prison cells, that you would be taken out of your cell and beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Every night several times. If half an hour passed by that was a good thing, before they would take me out again. This happened every single night, every single night.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was one of the individuals who was involved in these beatings -- involved in beating you named Marelja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. There was this man called Marelja. I learnt this, heard this, that is, from the guards of the HVO, who were standing two or three metres away and calmly looking at all this, watching it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was this individual named Marelja, was he one of the HVO guards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No, he wasn't an HVO guard. He wasn't from Busovaca. I didn't know him. Judging by the way he talked, I thought that he might be from Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did the HVO guards who were standing close by, did they ever take any steps to intervene or stop the beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Absolutely not. They didn't even try to do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, as a result of these multiple beatings that you suffered, what your body looked like after several days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: My jaw was broken. My head didn't have any bruises, but my jaw was broken and the entire -- the rest of my body was quite black. They were not bruises, but I was black all over from the beatings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did it come to your attention, during your stay in Kaonik, sir, that the people who were being taken and interrogated, that to your knowledge, these interrogations were taking place under the direction or supervision of Anto Sliskovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I'm one of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was personally taken away for interrogation to the building at the entrance into the camp where they interrogated me, two interrogators of the HVO police who were under the orders of Anto Sliskovic. Anto Sliskovic would also come at all times of the night, and he would interrogate individuals who were also taken out of their cells and taken to the building at the entrance and were interrogated by him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you relate to the Court anything that any of the HVO guards would say to you from time to time that made some reference to Mr. Sliskovic in terms of you being beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, there was all kinds of things. A young man who was a guard, for example, he looked like a child almost. When they took me out, I think he said something to this effect, "Well, you've done your bit. Anto Sliskovic is waiting for you and he'll finish you off."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did any of these HVO guards ever say to you something to the effect of, "Greetings from Anto Sliskovic"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, yes, that did happen. It's not the guards that said this --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who said it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: -- but that young man, the young man who took me out of the cell and beat me. After this orgy, he would send me kind regards from Anto Sliskovic, or kind regards from Vlado Cosic, or kind regards from somebody else, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you've already mentioned in passing that there was one particular beating incident where you were taken to another building, away from the hangar or prison cells, which was close to the entrance of the Kaonik Prison camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. At the very entrance to the camp. There's a building there. It is a high building. I was taken there with another young man, and that young man was taken up to the first floor before me and returned 15 minutes later and he was all beaten up. Then my turn came and they took me off to this first floor of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness J, before you continue with that, let me stay with the building, if I could, for another moment or two. At this time, had you gained any knowledge or information as any particular use that this building received or any particular unit or group that was stationed or used this building? Excuse me, stationed at or used that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. At the very entrance to the building there is a cell there. It is one metre by two metres, perhaps a little larger, and it has steel bars with no windows, and I was imprisoned there while the young man was taken up to the first floor. People would pass by, that is to say, HVO soldiers passed by the cell, and that was where their intervention platoon was located. Some 20 of them were there. So that they would bang on the bars and say, "You're the wrong nation," and use derogatory terms and swear at me and so forth. They said, "Balija."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you able to determine during this time who the commander, the on-site commander of this particular unit was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mirko Cosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How did that information come to your attention?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: I personally saw him. He was a policeman in ex-Yugoslavia, an experienced one, so that he was the commander there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell me, and I won't attempt the Bosnian language, but was the English translation of the unit he commanded, to your knowledge, something called the Punishment Intervention Squad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's what they called it, the Intervention Squad for emergency intervention. Anything that had to be done, they were the first there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, can you relate to the Court if you know, did you ever know of this Mirko Cosic having any association with Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know whether there was any association. I don't know what you mean exactly. Dario Kordic was the overall commander and they received orders from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "Association" is a poor word and it's probably my fault, especially perhaps with translation. I didn't mean in a family sense or a friendship sense, but do you know whether Mr. Cosic, for instance, was ever seen to be accompanying Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's have no leading questions about this sort of matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court whether you observed, at any time, the two individuals that you've just named together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: I couldn't say that I actually saw them together but that Mirko Cosic would pass by frequently, and the others, towards Tisovac. That was Kordic's headquarters, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. We'll leave it at that. We've touched on some of the other items in the next paragraph or two. The other individual who was taken with you on the same occasion was beaten and returned, and then you were taken to the first floor as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There were five HVO soldiers in the room at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, there were five soldiers. They all had their backs turned towards me as I came in or, rather, three of them, and two of them were facing me. I knew them. One was Petrovic and the other was Katava.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. So the record is clear, when you say "Petrovic," this is Zarko Petrovic, also times known as Tadija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the individual you referred to as "Katava," was his other name Zeljko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Zeljko, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You just said, I believe, you knew these men from before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I knew them personally, as they knew me. In fact, for a moment I was glad to see them, not knowing what would happen later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Both of these men were Croats and both of them at this time were wearing camouflage uniforms with HVO insignia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In your earlier testimony, is it correct, sir, that you identified both these men as men who worked for Anto Sliskovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. They were his closest associates, his right hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, on a table in the room, which some might describe as a table-tennis or a ping-pong table, there were a number of instruments, sticks, if you will, wooden, rubber, steel, police instruments on the table; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. There were many pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you then proceed to be questioned and beaten for the next approximately three hours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Petrovic and Katava were interrogating and the other three were beating with all kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was it at this time that your jaw was broken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. At one point this Marelja walked in, and he knocked me with his fist in the face and broke my jaw, upon which Katava -- no, not Katava, Tadija Petrovic cried out, "Not on the head." So after that they didn't hit me again on the head, but the rest of my body made up for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask the usher to please show the witness Exhibit 1862.1, and if you could put that on the ELMO, please. Let me make sure; 1862.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, you can really deal with these matters quickly. We've had these photographs or similar photographs before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will move through as quickly as I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if you would look at those, Witness J, and as the Court just directed, in the interests of time I'll simply ask you very specific and direction questions. This is an aerial photograph of the Kaonik camp. I don't think that there will be a dispute about that, I hope. There's a number 1 that has been marked, encircled and, in fact, are all the markings on this in terms of the 1, 2, 3 are markings that you previously made?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Number 1 is the hangar where we were locked up first; number 2 is the cells, the prison, with the cells; and number 3 is where I was taken, at the entrance to the camp, the building where they beat us and where we were interrogated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If I can next have the witness look, please, at 1861.1?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is the building at the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: With that photograph on the ELMO, can you point -- and you will have to do it so that it can be seen on the ELMO itself. The usher can assist you, please -- can you see the window or the room, on the outside, obviously, the exterior, where you were taken and actually beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's this one, this one here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: For purposes of the record, Your Honour, let it show that the witness is identifying the third window from the left of the picture on the first floor. All right. I think there are no other questions about the photograph, unless the Court has some.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, Witness J, I want to ask you about some other particular individuals in the next couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we get there, please. What is the relevance of these individuals, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, the relevance of these individuals, it is the Prosecution's view and position for purposes of the evidence in this case and ultimate argument, that the individuals named in the next several paragraphs are, the evidence will show, we believe, close associates or people who acted with or at the direction of Mr. Kordic. There are going to be a number of witnesses, not just Witness J, in addition to witnesses who have already testified, Your Honour, who are going to identify and talk about various people around Mr. Kordic, and I don't think anyone -- I don't think it is a secret to anyone at this point, that is not the nature of the Prosecution's case, at least not in very many instances, that Mr. Kordic would be seen doing the beating or doing the shooting or doing the burning but that Mr. Kordic, as most commanders and leaders do, had people who acted for him and at his direction, and it is going to be quite material to the Prosecution case to prove to the Court, ultimately we hope to the Court's satisfaction, who these lieutenants and associates and henchmen were, and that's the relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, take it quickly, please. I want, if at all possible, to finish this witness's evidence today. He has already been here for some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will move very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness J, did you know an individual, during your time in Busovaca, named Vlado Cosic and, in fact, was this Mirko's brother?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you know or, to your knowledge, at least, did you believe that this Mr. Cosic was the HVO chief of police in Busovaca in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he was under the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, based on your observation of him, whether he was seen or known to wear the letter "U", a metallic letter "U" on his hat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: He liked that, he liked a black uniform. He wore his weapon, like a cowboy, on one side, a knife on another. He wore a black beret with the letter "U" on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During this time in Central Bosnia, to your knowledge, what did the letter "U", at least in these circumstances, what did that stand for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was the symbol of the Ustasha movement, of fascism.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During this time, did you also know another individual named Gavro Maric, and can you tell the Court what you knew about Mr. Maric -- well, in the interests again, Your Honour, at the Court's direction, I will try. Did you know him to be previously a member in the Civil Defence under the former JNA structure and then subsequently, during the conflict in Central Bosnia in 1993, became the head of what you believed was a special Bosnian Croat military or police unit in the Busovaca area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Gavro Maric, in ex-Yugoslavia, worked in the Territorial Defence and the National Defence, but when the conflict broke out and when everything went downhill, he was one of the commanders in Kordic's units. I don't know exactly of what he was the commander, but he had a somewhat higher rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to Nikica Petrovic. Was he also, to your knowledge, an HVO police official in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you know him to have any particular role in connection with people's ability to come and go from the town of Busovaca in terms of movement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it quite like that. He was the coordinator for movement out of Busovaca and everything went through his hands regarding the few people who were left behind after the conflict who were still living in Busovaca. He was the only one who could grant permission for leaving or not leaving Busovaca. That's what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you have firsthand knowledge of this particular situation because of your father's attempt to leave Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And it -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: He tried many times and he was not granted permission to leave, and then, in the end, Anto Sliskovic gave him that permission. So that he left, at least according to his own account, at the very last minute; otherwise, he would have been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, based on your observation or knowledge, and I don't want you to speculate but based on observation or knowledge, can you tell the Court again what relationship, in terms of any command or control relationship that Mr. Petrovic had in relation to Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: In any army, including the HVO, it is quite clear, Kordic was the Number 1 man. Nothing happened without his knowledge nor was it possible to do anything without his knowledge. All these people were just clerks who were carrying out and implementing his ideas, his instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me go to one final one, please: Florijan Glavocevic. Is it correct that he was the president of something that you've called -- and I just want to make it clear, these are essentially the witness's words -- the Busovaca War Council; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct. It was set up and Florijan Glavocevic headed it, but his competencies were insignificant because absolutely nothing, nothing, absolutely nothing could he decide or do without Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the interests of what we are talking about, individuals, is it fair to say, Witness J, that you have no knowledge of and had no dealings with Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I don't know that man. I don't know. I never even heard anything about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Yes. Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When the witness said that Glavocevic couldn't do anything without Kordic's approval, is he speaking from his personal knowledge or from information that he received?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you answer the Court's question, Witness J? I mean, again, what do you base your assessment or statement on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Both on my personal experience and on events, the chronology of events in Busovaca. It was logical that such a man would be the Number 1. However, he, in fact, could do nothing. He could prevent nothing nor order anything. He could do absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So the record is clear, you're referring now to Florijan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So you're saying your physical observations of him, just to clarify your response to Judge Robinson's question, he was supposed to have a high position, and yet when you could see his actions in town --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, the witness is giving the evidence about these matters. Now, please, allow him to do it --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- rather than putting words into his mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies. I thought I was trying to help, but obviously I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you answer? Can you provide any more response to Judge Robinson's question, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I even had occasion, together with another Muslim, to go to Florijan's office in the municipality, where he received us very cordially, and we tried to talk about some things, to which he replied explicitly that he could do nothing without consulting Mr. Dario.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: May it please the Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: This was forecast in the papers preceding this trial, that the Prosecution's case of criminal association or criminal conspiracy, which is exactly what we heard a few minutes ago as to why these testimonies will be important, would be coming on by way of evidence, and it is problematic for all of us because it is a different evidentiary standard that is needed. We suddenly are suddenly responsible for the defence of individuals over whom we have no control or notice or who have not been indicted, they're essentially unindicted co-conspirators, and I'm just concerned that this continuing reference that Mr. Kordic was in charge of everything and everyone without a basis, without a specification, and done in a leading fashion, will require us to take on a burden that should not be on our shoulders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, you can cross-examine about all these matters, find out the basis upon which the witness gives his evidence. I have made sure that there are no leading questions about issues of this sort --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You certainly have, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- and I will continue to do so. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: However, Your Honour, the next series of questions, which are not going to name, I don't believe, Mr. Kordic -- according to the Court's direction, I will try to move quickly by leading questions until -- certainly until there is direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness J, would it be your testimony that while you were at Kaonik, you were taken, in the first instance, to dig trenches, and you were taken, in the first instance, for about three hours -- excuse me, I'm sorry. In the interests of speed, I'm getting ahead of myself. You were taking to a location near Putis and you dug trenches there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the guard at that particular location was Marko Krilic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. Marko Krilic was one of the guards in the prison --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: -- if you're referring to him, but in the field, he was not there. When we were taken to Putis, there were men, guards, wearing HVO uniforms from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, you're absolutely correct, obviously. Before you were taken out into the field, and this does go to the selection or calling-out process, can you tell the Court, did it appear to you that the trench-digging assignments had been organised in some detail when people like Mr. Krilic would show up during the day and call people out to be taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Clearly it was all organised. Lists were made as in the old days. It was known exactly who was in which group. The only thing we didn't know was where we would be sent. They came in with a certain list, and they called out from that list. Some of us were not called out but would be taken occasionally to go with a particular group.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. On this particular occasion, you were taken again out toward Putis, and you dug trenches there for about an entire day and into the evening and, in fact, until noon the next day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is exactly correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that, as you indicated, once you were released from Kaonik camp -- and "release" is not the right word, but turned over into the custody of this other group -- these were HVO soldiers different from the guards; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did they appear to be what people might describe as combat soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: All of them were under full combat gear with weapons at the ready pointed at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During this first trench-digging incident at Putis, the guards there -- excuse me -- well, the soldiers who were guarding you at that location were from Vitez, and you felt that on that particular occasion you were not terribly mistreated; is that correct? You were not mistreated other than the mistreatment that is part of being used to dig trenches, I suppose. Strike the question, Your Honour. It is not very well said. On that particular occasion, were you, apart from digging the trenches themselves, were you beaten or abused?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, none of our group was mistreated or beaten or anything on that day because these were soldiers from Vitez who treated us very correctly and fairly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, on that same day, did you also observe a group of 15 HVO soldiers set fire to 10 or to 15 houses on the road leading to Putis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Where we were digging, 15 soldiers went by under full combat gear, they went off towards the village of Putis and set fire to 10 to 15 houses, after which they returned or, rather, they passed by us again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The Court will note that we already touched on the next several paragraphs. I'm skipping to 159.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you were taken on a second occasion to dig trenches at another location called Kula, and at this incident, the conditions and events were much worse; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. On the 6th of February, 1993, I was taken to Kula, and as soon as I got there, my name was on a special piece of paper and I was called out, and from that moment on, it was hell.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you have knowledge as to where the HVO soldiers at Kula, people who you were under their guard, if you will, observation at that time, where these HVO soldiers were from, if you can tell or knew?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were some people from Busovaca, but those who did bad things and who mistreated us were not from Busovaca. They were unknown to me. One of them was, in fact, a Serb, because some people knew him personally. I think his name was Nedeljkovic or something like that. He was one of the worst, regarding the mistreatment and abuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: By the time you were taken to Kula on this occasion, did you already know, from other prisoners returning from other trench digging exercises, that Kula was known to be a particularly difficult location for prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Whenever a group returned from Kula, they were beaten up, with broken ribs, abused in various ways. So that people were really taking out -- venting their worst feelings on them. It is hard to imagine the things that they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you were taken to Kula and you were unloaded from the truck, you were taken, is it correct, and told to dig a trench about five centimetres away from a large beech tree; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. They told me to dig a trench close to a tree. It was 20 or 30 centimetres from a tree with a trunk which was 50 or 60 metres (sic) in diameter. It is a beech tree, as we call it, so it was impossible for me to dig so close, but they loved to watch me digging without really making any progress, especially as by then I had already been badly beaten up and didn't have much strength. So they derived a great deal of satisfaction from watching me. After some time, they let me dig in places where it was, in fact, possible to dig.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Before you continue on -- I hope there won't be an objection, Your Honour -- I believe the reference to the tree being "50 or 60 metres in diameter," is it correct, Witness J, that you meant "centimetres in diameter"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course. Fifty to sixty centimetres in diameter, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Let's try to move on. You were then taken from that location off to another place separate from the larger group. You were told to take off your clothes, which you did, except for an undergarment. This guard, this Serb that you named earlier, the person you believed to be a Serb, told you to sing a song that was insulting towards Croats; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. He took me behind this tree, this big oak tree. He told me to take my clothes off, I was left in an undergarment, and he then he ordered me to sing. As I probably wasn't singing loudly enough for him, then he continued beating me with the handle of a pick axe, ordering me to sing louder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As you sang the song louder, this song that was insulting towards Croats, did some of the Croat HVO soldiers come to you and hit you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Another two soldiers came and hit me mercilessly so that I would sing much more loudly this song, insulting song.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: They then took you and you continued to dig trenches, and is it true, Witness J, that around the middle of the day, three HVO soldiers came to you and attempted or pretended to burn your beard which you had at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is what they did. They made a torch from newspapers. As I had a beard, they lit it, accompanied by peals of laughter. To them it was joking, playing around with me. Then in the end later they took off my beret. As it was cold I always wore a hat, set fire to it. As it couldn't burn, it's made from such material that it was just scorched, that in the end they made me eat it and I actually did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Skipping over a few paragraphs, can you tell the Court whether, in the course of your being at Kula during this time and digging trenches and the things that you've told us about in the last few minutes, did you have occasion to complain to some of the HVO soldiers that you should not be treated-- that you and the others should not be treated the way that you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. At one point in time, one afternoon, Condra, I think his real name was Josip, though I worked in the same organisation as he did, but I'm not sure, and Mr. Gadarski, they came by. As we knew each other very well, I complained about the treatment and the things that were happening. They listened to me in a friendly manner, but their reply was that they would get in touch with Mr. Kordic to see whether anything could be improved for all of us prisoners and things that were being done to us while digging but that they could do nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Later on that same day, was there a situation where an HVO guard who was known as Hosovac came to you, took you up the hill with your shovel and pick axe, and told you then to dig a hole about 60 metres into the woods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. All day of this mistreatment and throughout that day they kept threatening with this person, whom they called Hosovac, that they would come, that darkness would fall, and that everything would be over, and that is what happened. He came as dark fell, and he took me some 50 or 60 metres away from the group uphill, allegedly to do some repair work. I had to take my shovel and pick axe, and he ordered me to dig. When I asked, "What am I digging?" As there were no trenches there. He said, "Just dig a hole. You're no fool. You know what you need to dig. Just dig a hole." So I thought that that was the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You thought you were digging your grave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Exactly. What else could it have been?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the witness could please be shown Exhibit 2116. If that could be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That is the patch that he wore on his sleeve.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This Hosovac would dress in a black uniform, with a black beret, with an insignia like the one in 2116 on his uniform; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, just so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. That's all on the photograph. Now, again to summarise these events, as events turned out, is it correct, sir, that you were able to essentially negotiate an agreement with this individual, to the end that if you agreed to give him two gold rings and some money that you had still been able to keep in your possession back at the Kaonik camp, and in return for that this man would protect you and the others during the rest of the time at Kula, and that was the agreement reached; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: (no interpretation) ... so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And he, in fact, did protect you and the others for that evening and the next day, and when you were taken back to Kaonik you, in fact, did give him the two rings some money; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: I gave him two rings and some money.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could the usher please show the witness Exhibit 1870.1? Could that be placed on the ELMO? Yes. I apologise, Your Honour. The highlight doesn't show up very well on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness J, if you look toward top of the exhibit on the ELMO, you will see some yellow highlighter. It's just been moved down, but the upper middle part of the page, do you see some yellow highlighter there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: (No audible response)

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court, is that the area around Putis where you were taken on the first trench digging exercise that you testified about this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, right there. From Strane towards Putis by Gavrine Kuce, along the main road to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just in the relationship to the town of Busovaca, if I direct you, if everyone in the courtroom looks down, directly below that, you will see the town of Busovaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's rather hard to see the town of Busovaca from Strane, from that side, at least from where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry witness, I didn't mean to say if you were physically standing in Strane, but in terms of the exhibit, the map --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the document speaks for itself, obviously, and about the six o'clock position is the town of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: To the right of that is some additional yellow highlighter. Is that the area around Kula where you were taken to dig trenches on the second occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. That concludes that exhibit. Witness J, can you please relate to the Court a particular situation where when you were being taken back to Kaonik from -- was it from Kula or from a Putis, an occasion where you were being taken back to Kaonik and your group was stopped? It was Kula? Can you relate to the Court, in your own words, what happened on that particular occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it was Putis. We were lined up in a column, which was quite normal. The guards were standing around us and they were taking us back to the camp, to Kaonik. On the bridge in Kaonik, coming towards us was a car, an U.N. vehicle, UNPROFOR or whichever, I can't know exactly what the signs on it were, but a reporter, a female reporter came out of the vehicle, and several armed people from the United Nations, and when asked by the first guard, the guard who was at the front asked where they were taking us, what they were doing to us, he just said, "Why are you asking me? Go and ask Kordic, because I've been brought here too."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, following the situation at Kula, was it the same day or the next day that it turned out that some prisoners who replaced you, excuse me, some Muslim prisoners who replaced you at Kula in trench digging, that it came to your attention, as the information came back to the camp, that several of them had been killed while trench digging?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. There were 30 of us who were returned to the camp again, and several new prisoners took our place at Kula. So that was on the 7th of February. They too were returned on the morning of the 8th of February from Kula, and they had all been beaten and were unrecognisable. Two of them, in fact, three of them were killed, had been killed. They did not return, that is. Jasmin Sehovic, Elezovic Nermin, and I think Mustafa. He was, I think, from somewhere around Kacuni. They were not returned. So that this exchange, the exchange that was to have taken place on the 8th of February, was late because three people were missing, and they had to be missing because they had been killed. So the Red Cross insisted that they be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, Witness J, we've probably jumped a bit ahead of ourselves. To put your testimony in context, let's go back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, we need to take a break shortly. Are you coming to the end?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very much the end, Your Honour. I think there's about ten questions left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn for a quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness J, you had learned some days preceding the 8th of February, 1993, that there was going to be a prisoner exchange, an exchange between the HVO and Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I was about to ask you before the recess that you had been -- Kaonik had been visited by the Red Cross, the International Red Cross, on about the 2nd of February, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct. We were all registered by the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could have the usher please show you Exhibit 2716, which you can see on the ELMO there, sir, to your right -- well, you have the B/C/S version in front of you or on the ELMO. Is that the Red Cross certification or certificate or a copy of that concerning your being seen at Kaonik on approximately February 2nd, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me note for the record and ask that this exhibit be kept and placed under seal because obviously it bears the name of the witness, who is protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: To your knowledge, Witness J, was the Red Cross allowed to see, in fact, all of the actual conditions at Kaonik camp on the 2nd of February, 1993, or, to your knowledge, was it a situation that the individual prisoners were just taken to a central location where they could be seen by a Red Cross representative?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, in the hallway between the cells, tables were set up, and that's where we had our lunch, we ate our food there, and that is where some of us were allowed to talk to the officials of the Red Cross, to exchange a few words with them, whereas all the rest of us just filled in forms in order to be registered by the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, because of my question, sir, we jumped ahead, and I apologise. You had mentioned a few minutes ago that there was a group of Muslim prisoners taken from Kaonik to replace your work detail, if you will, when it was brought back to Kaonik, and it was during or among that group that two or three Muslim prisoners had been killed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did it come to your attention that later that day, or approximately 5.00 the next morning, if you will, you awoke to the sound of someone or some persons being beaten out in the corridor near your cell; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It occurred in the corridor between our cells, because there were cells on both sides, and you could hear cries and blows, that somebody was being beaten; and when I beat on the door to ask to be excused to go to the toilet, one of the guards came and -- that was what we usually did when we wanted to go to the toilet. I saw that the HVO police, led by Babic, Nikesa Babic - Nikesa is his nickname, I don't know his actual name - but I saw that they were beating that Hos man and two other people from Kula, and they were the ones who had maltreated us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say, so the record is clear, "that Hos man," was this the individual you described earlier as Hosovac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, from Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As you observed this and talked among yourselves, can you tell the Court any understanding that you came to as to why these HVO soldiers were being beaten or appeared to be being beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: At Kula during that particular night, some of the HVO guards became frightened as to what had happened to those young men and that finally two of them were actually killed and perhaps a third one too, but two were certainly killed, Jasmin Sehovic and Nermin Elezovic, in a very terrible way, so that the HVO police came and took them to the prison. However, some gold and some money that was found on them was to be returned to us later on, but that is a drop in the ocean compared to what was all taken away, and this seemed like a good piece of acting to us because, by what those who stayed in the prison told us, those people were released the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you come to any conclusion whether you believed that, in fact, the HVO police, the military police, wanted the Muslims to see or to think that these people were being punished?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Well, yes, that was quite obvious. They wanted to show us that they were just and that they were doing things in the right way and that they had everything under control. That was the object of it all. That was their proof.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
